analysis.one_liner: Repeals the health law's limits on hospitals owned by the doctors who refer patients to them.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would repeal ACA limits on physician-owned hospitals, never got a hearing or a vote and died at the end of the 112th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The ACA barred most new physician-owned hospitals from Medicare and put limits — on conflicts of interest, patient safety, and expansion — on a small exception for existing rural-provider hospitals. This bill would erase those limits and restore the rules as if the ACA had never passed, letting doctors refer Medicare patients to hospitals they have a financial stake in. The bill went to two House committees and their health subcommittees, where it sat without a hearing, a markup, or a vote until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Physician-investors who own hospitals. The bill would let their facilities keep Medicare participation and expand without the ACA's conflict-of-interest, investment, and expansion limits, protecting the revenue they earn from referrals by their own doctors.

how_it_helps.text: It restores previous law as if the ACA had never touched it, allowing physician-owned hospitals grandfathered under the ACA's rural-provider exception to keep participating in Medicare without the ACA's conflict-of-interest, investment, patient-safety, and expansion-limit requirements
It wipes out the ACA's authority to limit how much physician-owned hospitals can expand, letting doctor-owners grow their facilities and their referral revenue

analysis.who_pays: Medicare patients and taxpayers. Doctor-owned hospitals create a financial incentive for physicians to refer patients to facilities they profit from, and the ACA's expansion limits were designed to contain that; the bill would remove them.

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals requirements Congress had imposed on physician-owned hospitals to address conflicts of interest, protect patient safety, and limit their expansion — safeguards aimed at the financial incentive for doctors to send patients to hospitals they own

It rolls back part of the ACA's conflict-of-interest rules, restoring pre-2010 law in which doctors could profit from referring their own Medicare patients to hospitals in which they hold an investment

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the physician-investors the bill restores a valuable business opportunity, but the cost falls on Medicare patients and taxpayers in the form of referrals to physician-owned facilities, higher utilization, and the conflict-of-interest questions that led Congress to restrict these hospitals in the first place. The bill as written rolls back all the conflict-of-interest, investment, and expansion safeguards the ACA put in place, with nothing replacing them.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees and their health subcommittees, and neither ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 17, 2011 and referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees
Within a week it was referred to the Health Subcommittee in each committee, but no hearings, markups, or floor votes followed
It died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, without ever getting a vote in either chamber

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Patients and the ACA's conflict-of-interest safeguards survive; physician-investors gain nothing from the repeal.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The ACA's limits stayed; nothing changed

for.name: Rep. Sam Johnson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the ACA's limits on physician-owned hospitals

sides.party_line_note: All sponsorship and cosponsorship was Republican except for three Democrats; no committee or floor action ever occurred, so no votes reveal broader support.

industries.note: The bill restores their ability to participate in Medicare and expand without the ACA's conflict-of-interest, patient-safety, and expansion limits. Their gain comes through Medicare payments for patients their own doctors refer to facilities they own.
Physician-owned competitors siphoning referrals and profitable patients cuts into community hospitals' revenue; they supported the ACA restrictions this bill would repeal.
